analysis.one_liner: Penalizes companies that misclassify employees as contractors and requires written notice of worker classification.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee markup or a floor vote; its only House actions were referrals, and it died when the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required companies that use contractors to keep records on them and give each worker written notice of their classification, with a statement telling workers how to contact the Department of Labor if they suspect they were wrongly labeled a contractor. It would have made misclassification itself unlawful, doubled back-pay penalties when it accompanied wage violations, set civil fines of up to $5,000 per repeat violation, and required state unemployment programs to audit for unregistered employers and unreported wages.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers misclassified as independent contractors, who lose minimum wage, overtime, and unemployment coverage under contractor status. Compliant employers also benefit, because rivals could no longer undercut them by misclassifying workers to cut labor costs.

how_it_helps.text: Requires companies to keep records of contractor workers and give each new employee and contractor written notice of their classification, including a statement directing workers to contact the Department of Labor if they suspect misclassification [S2, S3].

Makes it unlawful to fail to classify a worker accurately and creates a presumption that a worker is an employee when the employer has not kept the required records or given the required notice, rebuttable only by clear and convincing evidence [S2, S3].

Doubles liquidated damages for minimum wage and maximum hours violations when the employer also misclassified the worker, and sets civil penalties up to $1,100 per violation, or up to $5,000 for repeat or willful violations [S2, S3].

Protects workers from being fired or retaliated against for challenging their classification, and requires every Department of Labor office that discovers misclassification to report it to the Wage and Hour Division, which may share the information with the IRS [S2, S3].

Requires state unemployment programs, as a condition of federal grants, to audit for employers who fail to register or pay unreported wages in ways that exclude workers from unemployment coverage, and to impose administrative penalties for misclassification [S2, S3].

Directs the Labor Department to conduct targeted audits of industries with frequent misclassification and to build a public webpage summarizing workers' rights in plain language and multiple languages [S2, S3].

analysis.who_pays: Companies that rely on classifying workers as independent contractors, including gig-style operations, subcontractors, and staffing arrangements, through recordkeeping duties, notice requirements, per-violation fines, and doubled back-pay liability. Some costs could reach consumers as higher prices for services.

drawbacks.text: The recordkeeping and notice duties apply to every non-employee engaged for labor or services, adding paperwork for small businesses and for firms that use genuinely independent contractors [S3].

The presumption of employee status, rebuttable only by clear and convincing evidence, raises the stakes of any classification dispute and could make it harder for businesses to defend a legitimate contractor arrangement, even where the worker prefers independence [S3].
Higher compliance costs and liability would fall hardest on low-margin businesses that use subcontractor models, and could reduce flexible contractor arrangements some workers value.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: misclassification strips minimum wage, overtime, and unemployment coverage from a large number of workers, and the bill attacks it with notice, records, penalties, and audits. The cost side is genuine too, because the paperwork burden and the clear-and-convincing rebuttal standard would touch businesses that classify correctly, and enforcement costs would fall on the Labor Department and state unemployment agencies. On balance, a well-designed enforcement bill whose main burden falls on firms whose business model depends on the misclassification itself.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and then to subcommittees, never received a markup or a vote, and died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Rep. Lynn Woolsey, joined by Reps. Robert Andrews and George Miller, introduced the bill on October 13, 2011 [S1, S3].
The House referred it to the Education and the Workforce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced [S5].
Within a week it was referred to a Ways and Means subcommittee, and in November to the Education and the Workforce Subcommittee on Workforce Protections [S5].
No further action appears in the record: no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote occurred before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S1, S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Businesses that depend on treating workers as independent contractors were better off, because the new notice duties, fines, doubled damages, and unemployment audits never took effect. State unemployment agencies avoided new audit and penalty conditions. Misclassified workers gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: All 32 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republicans sponsored or backed the bill, and the Republican-led committees never acted on it.

industries.industry: Gig, delivery, and other independent-contractor-dependent businesses
industries.note: The bill would have made misclassification unlawful, imposed per-worker penalties of up to $5,000 for repeat violations, and doubled back-pay damages, directly threatening business models built on treating employees as contractors. Those models shift minimum wage, overtime, and unemployment costs onto workers.

industries.industry: Construction, trucking, and subcontracting/staffing firms with frequent misclassification
industries.note: The Labor Department was directed to run targeted audits in industries with frequent misclassification, and state unemployment agencies were required to audit unregistered employers and unreported wages in these sectors. These industries would face heightened enforcement exposure.

Compliant employers currently compete against rivals who cut labor costs by misclassifying workers; the bill would have narrowed that gap. Its recordkeeping and notice duties would have added some paperwork for them as well.

States would have had to build audit programs and penalties as a condition of federal grants, an administrative cost, but misclassification shrinks the unemployment tax base and leaves workers without benefits, so closing it strengthens the system's funding.
